topics: 💰 Selling Rights to Future Fetuses — permitted when the mother isn't yet pregnant
⚖️ Two Versions of the Penalty — 10× or 100× the value for selling an animal or a slave to a gentile
📜 'All the Firstborn' — the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda read the same verse to opposite conclusions
🐑 How Much Gentile Ownership Exempts? — an ear (Rav Huna) vs. a life-sustaining limb (Rav Ḥisda, Rava)
📖 Two Case Stories — the convert's cattle and Rav Mari bar Raḥel's fatal shortcut
🍼 New Mishna: Priests and Levites — exempt from redeeming their own firstborn donkeys, a fortiori from the wilderness

overview.title: 📖 Overview: From Penalties to the Verse Itself
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 3a–3b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by resolving yesterday's dilemma: it is indeed permitted to sell a gentile only the rights to an animal's future fetuses, so long as the animal is not yet pregnant. The Gemara then compares penalties for improperly selling an animal or a slave to a gentile, before turning to the theoretical heart of the mishna's rule: what does the phrase 'sanctify to Me all the firstborn' (Exodus 13:2) actually teach, and how much gentile ownership is enough to exempt an animal? Two real cases test the limits of the leniency, and the daf closes with a new mishna: priests and Levites need not redeem their own firstborn donkeys.

slides.title: 💰 Selling to a Gentile: Two Versions of the Penalty
slides.subtitle: Reish Lakish vs. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and the amount they set
headers: Sells a slave (R' Yehoshua ben Levi)
rows: Buy it back for up to 10× its value
Buy him back for up to 100× its value — a slave loses mitzvot every day he serves a gentile
Buy it back for up to 100× its value
Buy him back for up to 10× its value — a slave is uncommon, so the Sages did not decree as severely for him

callout.label: Why receivership is lighter:
callout.text: A sale severs the animal entirely from the Jew (פָּסְקָה מִינֵּיהּ); giving it in receivership does not — the Jew still owns it — so that penalty stays at ten times, regardless of which version of the sale-penalty is correct.

slides.title: 📜 'All the Firstborn' — One Verse, Two Readings
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yehoshua: both the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda interpret the same verse (Exodus 13:2)

lines.speaker: Rabbis
lines.text: Plain 'the firstborn' would mean even a partial firstborn is obligated. So the Torah writes 'all' — teaching it is obligated only when the entire animal belongs to a Jew.

lines.speaker: R' Yehuda
lines.text: Plain 'the firstborn' would mean only a fully Jewish-owned firstborn is obligated. So the Torah writes 'all' — teaching it is obligated even if any amount belongs to a Jew.

lines.speaker: Alt. read
lines.text: Or say: everyone agrees plain 'the firstborn' means a majority-owned firstborn is obligated.

lines.speaker: Alt. read
lines.text: And they disagree only whether 'all' comes to fill the requirement up to the whole animal, or to reduce it down to any share at all.

callout.label: Stakes:
callout.text: This dispute is the theoretical engine behind the mishna's rule that a firstborn donkey is exempt whenever a gentile has any share in it.

slides.title: 🐑 How Much Gentile Ownership Is Enough to Exempt?
slides.subtitle: Three opinions on the threshold, per the Rabbis' view

boxes.title: Rav Huna
items: Even the animal's ear alone, if gentile-owned, exempts it
Rav Naḥman objects: then let the priest tell the gentile, 'take your ear and go'

boxes.title: Rav Ḥisda
items: Only a limb that, if removed, would immediately render the animal a carcass (נְבֵלָה)
A merely important limb is not enough

boxes.title: Rava
items: Only a limb that, if removed, would eventually render it a tereifa

callout.label: Rav Pappa's harmonization:
callout.text: No dispute at all — Rav Huna's lenient 'even an ear' speaks about the fetus itself (which needs 'all the firstborn' to be Jewish); Rav Ḥisda and Rava speak about the mother.

slides.title: 📖 Two Case Stories Testing the Leniency
slides.subtitle: One ends in a simple ruling; the other ends badly

steps.content: 1️⃣ A female convert's gentile brothers gave her animals to fatten, splitting the profits. She asked Rava about firstborn status.
2️⃣ Rava ruled: exempt — no one is concerned for Rabbi Yehuda's stricter view that a gentile-partnership animal is obligated
3️⃣ Rav Mari bar Raḥel transferred ownership of just his firstborns' ears to a gentile, yet still barred shearing or labor and gave them to priests

4️⃣ His animals ultimately died — either because he abrogated their sanctity unnecessarily, or because others copied his transfer without completing it properly and came to mishandle their own firstborns

callout.label: Lesson:
callout.text: A leniency that works only through a precise, completed legal transaction is dangerous to rely on in practice — others may imitate the result without the mechanism.

slides.title: 🍼 New Mishna: Priests and Levites Need Not Redeem Their Firstborn Donkeys
slides.subtitle: An a fortiori (קַל וָחוֹמֶר) argument from the census in the wilderness

nodes.content: ❓ Why are priests and Levites exempt from redeeming their own firstborn donkeys?
📜 In the wilderness: 'Take the Levites in exchange for all the firstborn among the children of Israel, and the animal of the Levites in exchange for their animals' (Numbers 3:45)
✅ If the Levites' substitution exempted the firstborns and donkeys of all Israel in the wilderness, all the more so it exempts their own firstborn donkeys now

summary.principle: The mishna's rule — that a firstborn is obligated only when it belongs entirely to a Jew — flows from competing readings of 'all the firstborn' (Exodus 13:2), and even a slight, properly-transacted gentile share is enough to exempt it.

flowSteps.content: 💰 Resolved: selling only future fetuses is permitted if the animal isn't yet pregnant; penalties for improper sales run 10× or 100× value
📜 Core dispute: does 'all the firstborn' require total Jewish ownership (Rabbis) or include even partial ownership (R' Yehuda)?

columns.content: 🐑 Threshold to exempt: an ear (Rav Huna) vs. a life-sustaining limb (Rav Ḥisda, Rava) — reconciled as fetus vs. mother
📖 Rav Mari bar Raḥel's partial-ear leniency backfired when others copied it incorrectly

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: priests and Levites are exempt from redeeming their own firstborn donkeys — a fortiori from their wilderness role redeeming all of Israel's

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's resolution, when is it permitted to sell a gentile only the rights to an animal's future offspring?
o: Only if the animal is not yet pregnant
Only if the animal is already pregnant
It is never permitted
Only on Shabbat eve
quiz.e: The baraita's prohibition refers to an already-pregnant animal (an existing fetus); selling future offspring-rights in an animal not yet pregnant is permitted.

quiz.q: In the first version of the dispute, why is the penalty for selling a slave to a gentile (100×) harsher than for selling an animal (10×)?
o: Slaves are worth more money
A slave is restricted from performing mitzvot every day he remains with the gentile
Animals can be redeemed more easily
There is no difference between the two
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that a slave sold to a gentile is prevented from fulfilling mitzvot every single day, justifying a much steeper penalty than for an animal.

quiz.q: According to the Rabbis' reading of Exodus 13:2, what does the word 'all' ('all the firstborn') come to teach?
o: That even a small Jewish share obligates the firstborn
That the firstborn is obligated only if the entire animal belongs to a Jew
That only firstborn donkeys are included
That the word is extraneous and teaches nothing
quiz.e: The Rabbis hold that without the word 'all,' even partial Jewish ownership would obligate the animal; 'all' comes to require total Jewish ownership.

quiz.q: According to Rav Huna, how much gentile ownership in a firstborn fetus is enough to exempt it from firstborn status?
o: At least half the animal
The entire animal
Even just its ear
Only a life-sustaining limb
quiz.e: Rav Huna rules that even gentile ownership of only the fetus's ear is sufficient to exempt it, though Rav Naḥman raises an objection to this.

quiz.q: How did Rava rule for the female convert whose gentile brothers gave her animals to fatten in exchange for a share of the profits?
o: The firstborns were fully obligated
The firstborns were exempt, since no one follows Rabbi Yehuda's stricter opinion about gentile partnerships
She had to ask the gentile brothers first
The animals had to be given entirely to the priest
quiz.e: Rava told her the firstborns were exempt, explaining that no one is concerned with Rabbi Yehuda's minority view that a gentile-partnership animal is obligated in firstborn status.
